title: Chapter 2. The Sea That Is Not This One

blocks.text: The second letter didn't bring a plain. It brought water.
blocks.html: The second letter didn't bring a plain. It brought water.

blocks.text: Andrés was on the doorstep, coffee in hand, when the Mar Menor suddenly stopped being enough for his eyes. He felt another shore under his feet: not lagoon sand, but a dark, warm tongue of land that didn't wet you the way things wet you here. The water of that world wasn't entirely salty, or it was salty in a different way, as if someone had mixed honey and metal and a flower that doesn't exist on Earth. It smelled of warm rain and of something sweet, almost like figs, and it moved with the slowness of a large animal breathing.

blocks.text: The other Andrés was in a vessel that wasn't his six-metre boat, and yet he steered it with the same shoulders, with the same attention of someone who has learned to read a plate of water. The sky was pale yellow, not blue, and there was no east or west wind he recognised: a uniform brightness, like an endless dusk, spilled over a sea that never ended. There was no land in sight. Only, here and there, low islands made not of rock but of a living mat, a kind of raft of broad leaves and interwoven roots, which rose and fell with the breathing of the water.

blocks.text: On one of those rafts there were beings. Andrés, the one in Lo Pagán, saw them without having seen them, and found it hard to accept them, the way you accept a dream that doesn't ask permission. They weren't people. Nor were they the machines of the Eden along the shore. They were tall and slow, a colour somewhere between reed and ash, with arms that were too long and a chest that opened and closed, gently, to the rhythm of the sea. They didn't speak. They sang, if that was singing: a deep, wet murmur that got into Andrés's bones the way the wind gets into you when it comes into the house.

blocks.text: The clone didn't raise a weapon. He hadn't come to conquer. He took off his helmet, because the air was breathable, and let the song reach his face. One of the beings came closer and touched the edge of the vessel with a broad finger, and in that contact (Andrés felt it in his knuckles) there was an image, not a word: the sea seen from below, full of slow lights, as if someone had sown stars in the water and the stars had learned to graze.

blocks.text: *It's a sea,* thought the one who searched, and the one on the shore thought it with him, with an almost childlike relief. *There are worlds with water. Not all of them are red stone.*

blocks.text: Then came the homesickness, which gives no warning. The clone, in the middle of that warm immensity, missed the stillness of the Mar Menor: the plate, the nearby shore, the way that here the water doesn't need to be infinite to be enough. And Andrés, on the doorstep, his cup still warm, missed a sea he had never sailed, a song he had never heard with these ears, a yellow sky that didn't belong to him. He felt dizzy for a moment, not from waves, but from that double and clean envy, without malice, of someone who wants to be in both places and can't.

blocks.text: His coffee cooled for more than half a minute. Aya, behind him, saw the cup tilt and steadied it, the way you steady something about to fall.

blocks.text: “Another world,” he said, when he could. “A sea. It isn't this one. It's bigger. And I, the other one, was in a boat that isn't mine, and I steered it just the same. There are… people. They didn't hurt us. They sang.”

blocks.text: Aya heard the song in his telling, not in her chip. She closed her eyes, as if she could lend it the hearing the bridge didn't give her.

blocks.text: “Did you stay in the boat?” she asked.
blocks.html: “Did you stay in the boat?” she asked.

blocks.text: “He did. I stayed here. But my hands taste of that water. And this one,” he said, pointing at the lagoon, which at that hour was beginning to shine, “suddenly seems like a glass to me.”
blocks.html: “He did. I stayed here. But my hands taste of that water. And this one,” he said, pointing at the lagoon, which at that hour was beginning to shine, “suddenly seems like a glass to me.”

blocks.text: He regretted it as he said it. The Mar Menor wasn't a glass. It was his home. It was the road of his mornings, the tin, the flamingos, the trade. Asking it to be that other sea was like asking a cracked cup to be a pitcher. The cup is enough, if you drink from it truly.

blocks.text: That afternoon, Lía took him for a walk through El Estacio, slowly, the way you walk someone who has just stepped off a ship and hasn't got his weight right yet. The water of home was close by, faithful, shallow, wounded and beautiful, stubborn. A girl waved from a garden tended by humanoids, and Lía raised her hand, because in Lo Pagán people greeted one another again.

blocks.text: “Father,” she said, “what is it to live something without living it?”
blocks.html: “Father,” she said, “what is it to live something without living it?”

blocks.text: Andrés looked at his own feet on the promenade, firm on this earth, and at the memory of the other's feet on the living mat.
blocks.html: Andrés looked at his own feet on the promenade, firm on this earth, and at the memory of the other's feet on the living mat.

blocks.text: “It's finding out about a hunger you can't sit down at the table,” he said. “And it's also a stroke of luck. I'm not going to that sea. He isn't coming back to this shore this afternoon. Each of us has what the other lacks. Maybe that's why both things hurt at once.”

blocks.text: Lía smiled, and the smile stayed thoughtful on her face, the smile of a grown woman who doesn't close the matter.
blocks.html: Lía smiled, and the smile stayed thoughtful on her face, the smile of a grown woman who doesn't close the matter.

blocks.text: “MAY wouldn't give an opinion,” she said. “She'd leave the question. Eva would ask whether hunger stops being hunger because it belongs to someone else. I'll ask you only this: when you go out in your boat again, will you be going out onto this water, or the other?”
blocks.html: “MAY wouldn't give an opinion,” she said. “She'd leave the question. Eva would ask whether hunger stops being hunger because it belongs to someone else. I'll ask you only this: when you go out in your boat again, will you be going out onto this water, or the other?”

blocks.text: He didn't know yet. The next day he found out, or came close. He went out at dawn, when the lagoon was flat as a plate and the sky was brightening in the east. The engine made the same noise as always. The nets, the same weight. And while he fished, the letter didn't come back. There was only this sea, his own, the one outsiders don't know how to name, and it was enough for him, and at times it wasn't, and both truths fitted in the same body, which is what truths tend to do when you insist on being only one person.

blocks.text: At dusk, the clone (beneath that other yellow sky) approached a larger raft, where the song was deeper. A being offered him, with the same broad finger, a bowl of water from its sea. The clone drank. Andrés, in Lo Pagán, swallowed, and the taste of figs and metal stayed with him until night, on top of the usual taste of salt, like two meals that don't quarrel and don't quite mix either.

blocks.text: Aya made him his coffee. She let it cool for half a minute. She looked him in the eyes.

blocks.text: “Are you here?”
blocks.html: “Are you here?”

blocks.text: “I'm here,” he said. “And he's in a water that isn't this one. And I've drunk it without drinking it. I don't know what to call it, Aya. It isn't betrayal. It's a visit. But visits, when they come in so deep, never quite leave.”

blocks.text: She rested her forehead against his temple, a small gesture, a home gesture.
blocks.html: She rested her forehead against his temple, a small gesture, a home gesture.

blocks.text: “Their not quite leaving isn't the same as pushing you out,” she said. “This shore has room. There's room for the coffee, for the letter, for you. If one day there wasn't room for you, tell me. And we'll talk about it, the way you talk about what matters: with no protocol and no hurry.”

blocks.text: In the chip, Eva let fall, softly, the question Aya didn't voice:
blocks.html: In the chip, Eva let fall, softly, the question Aya didn't voice:

blocks.text: *If a man drinks two seas, to which does he owe his thirst?*
blocks.html: If a man drinks two seas, to which does he owe his thirst?

blocks.text: MAY added no judgment. Only the fact, beside it, like a glass:
blocks.html: MAY added no judgment. Only the fact, beside it, like a glass:

blocks.text: *There is a water that wets the shirt and a water that wets only the memory. In the language of this house, both are called sea.*
blocks.html: There is a water that wets the shirt and a water that wets only the memory. In the language of this house, both are called sea.

blocks.text: That night Andrés dreamed of the living rafts and woke with dry sheets. He got up, went to the doorstep and looked at the Mar Menor. The water was black and still. It didn't sing like that other one. It sang in its own way, older, lower, the way it always had. He spoke to it, not out of madness but out of habit, as he had spoken to it on the day of his return:

It didn't sing like that other one. It sang in its own way, older, lower, the way it always had. He spoke to it, not out of madness but out of habit, as he had spoken to it on the day of his return:

blocks.text: “You're this one. The other is the other. I'm staying, even if its taste reaches me.”
blocks.html: “You're this one. The other is the other. I'm staying, even if its taste reaches me.”

blocks.text: The murmur against the shore didn't change. It had no reason to. The sea of home, which is neither quite sea nor quite land, doesn't argue with those who stay. It holds them up. And that, for a fisherman who had just drunk a world, was still, and once again, enough to live on.
